outcome: No proof or counterexample of the general statement has appeared since 26 January 2024 in any source I could reach; the only in-window work bearing on it re-proves the already-known large-field case (Kaplan, Matthews and Walsberg, arXiv 2607.16942, 18 July 2026), and the one AI-credited counterexample from 2026 (Freitag and Mutchnik, arXiv 2609.00436) concerns the stable forking conjecture, a different problem.
problem_asks: One universal claim with three parts: (1) every infinite field K; (2) whose complete first-order theory in the language of rings is stable; (3) is separably closed. It quantifies over all characteristics and all imperfection degrees and adds no other hypothesis. Not asked: the converse (every separably closed field is stable), which is known from Ershov and Wood.

events.what_happened: Macintyre showed that every infinite omega-stable field (aleph-0-stable in the wording of Johnson, Tran, Walsberg and Ye) is algebraically closed. Published as omega-1-categorical fields, Fundamenta Mathematicae, 1971. I did not open the original; the result is stated in the introduction of arXiv 2009.02319, which I did open.
events.delivers: For the omega-stable class only: every infinite omega-stable field is algebraically closed, which is stronger than separably closed, so the statement holds for that class.
events.remains: Every infinite stable field that is not omega-stable. That is the whole statement outside the omega-stable class.

checked_by.qualification: Journal of record for the 1971 publication
checked_by.what_they_did: Published the paper in 1971. I did not confirm this from the paper; the statement is taken from the JTWY introduction.

events.direction: Confirms the statement for the omega-stable class, with the stronger conclusion of algebraic closure.

events.what_happened: Cherlin and Shelah showed that every infinite superstable field is algebraically closed (Superstable fields and groups, Annals of Mathematical Logic 18 (1980), 227-270, per a search snippet). The statement is taken from the JTWY introduction, which I opened; the 1980 paper itself was not opened.
events.delivers: For the superstable class only: every infinite superstable field is algebraically closed, so the statement holds for that class.
events.remains: Every infinite stable field that is not superstable. Wood (1979, per a search snippet) showed that separably closed fields are stable but not superstable, so the imperfect separably closed fields lie entirely in the part that remains open.

checked_by.who: Annals of Mathematical Logic (referee not identified)
checked_by.qualification: Journal of record for the 1980 publication
checked_by.what_they_did: Published the paper in 1980. Not confirmed from the paper.

events.direction: Confirms the statement for the superstable class, with the stronger conclusion of algebraic closure.

events.what_happened: Poizat showed that an infinite bounded stable field is separably closed (bounded meaning finitely many separable extensions of each degree). Stated in Dave Marker's 2020-2021 lecture notes, which I could not read. Year 1983 comes from a secondary citation (a 1983 Poizat lemma) that I did not open, so treat the year as unverified. The same source also attributes to Poizat: a stable field is either separably closed or has infinitely many extensions of each degree n.
events.delivers: For the bounded class only: every infinite bounded stable field is separably closed. Also, as attributed, a dichotomy for stable fields: separably closed, or infinitely many extensions of each degree n.
events.remains: Every infinite stable field that is unbounded, which covers the whole non-bounded part of the statement.
events.doubts: The year and the exact source for the bounded result are unverified; the bounded convention also differs between sources (Pillay and Walsberg note that some authors use bounded in a broader sense).
events.direction: Confirms the statement for the bounded class.

events.what_happened: Thomas Scanlon posted a note on his web page, 'Infinite stable fields are Artin-Schreier closed', proving that for an infinite stable field of characteristic p > 0 the map x to x^p - x is surjective, so there are no finite Galois extensions of degree divisible by p. Kaplan, Scanlon and Wagner state that the note was published on Scanlon's web page in 1999 (opened, arXiv 1009.5421). The note's PDF could not be read through WebFetch, so the content is taken from the citing paper and a search snippet. A search snippet also says a corrected version thanks Anand Pillay for pointing out an error in an earlier version.
events.revisions: Per a search snippet of the note's own page (not opened): a corrected version, thanking Pillay for pointing out an error in an earlier version. I could not read the PDF to check the dates of versions.
events.delivers: Partial, characteristic p only: an infinite stable field of characteristic p has the Artin-Schreier property, that x to x^p - x is surjective, so it has no finite Galois extension of degree divisible by p. Separably closed fields of characteristic p have this property too, but it does not imply separable closure.
events.remains: Characteristic 0 entirely. In characteristic p, the conclusion that the field is separably closed.

checked_by.who: Itay Kaplan, Thomas Scanlon and Frank O. Wagner
checked_by.qualification: Model theorists who worked on the same kind of question
checked_by.what_they_did: Extended the Artin-Schreier argument to NIP fields and, in 2006, to simple fields (Israel Journal of Mathematics 185 (2011)). This is an extension of the method, not a check of the stable-field case.

events.doubts: A search snippet says an earlier version of the note contained an error, which Scanlon corrected after Pillay pointed it out. Not a withdrawal. I could not read the current version.
events.direction: Partial step in characteristic p: an Artin-Schreier property that every separably closed field of characteristic p also has.

events.what_happened: Duret showed (a) that a PAC field which is not separably closed has the independence property, and (b) that the simple fields conjecture implies the stable fields conjecture, because a PAC field is stable if and only if it is separably closed. Cited in the Halevi-Hasson-Jahnke survey (opened, arXiv 1805.03814), which says Duret, in [7], has shown (b). Chatzidakis's 2008 Leeds notes describe (a) (search snippet, not opened). The original paper was not located, so the date is not established.
events.delivers: Conditional only: if the simple fields conjecture (every infinite simple field is a bounded PAC field) holds, then the stable fields conjecture holds. Also: non-separably-closed PAC fields have the independence property.
events.remains: The stable fields statement itself, since the implication runs from an open conjecture.
events.direction: Reduces the stable fields statement to the simple fields conjecture. Does not settle the statement.

events.what_happened: Krupinski and Pillay, 'On stable fields and weight' (arXiv 0909.5623, posted September 2009; the PDF header is dated 30 September 2009 per a search snippet). Journal of the Institute of Mathematics of Jussieu 10(2) (2011), 349-358; the journal record gives received 24 October 2009 and accepted 3 February 2010 (search snippet, not opened). The paper proves that an infinite stable field whose generic type has weight 1 is separably closed (Theorem 1.7: each stable field of weight 1 is separably closed). Corollary 2.2: for an infinite stable field of finite weight, K^q = K for all but finitely many primes q, with at most w such primes when the weight is w. It also gives partial results for strongly stable fields, where every type has finite weight. Read from the arXiv HTML mirror (ar5iv).
events.revisions: arXiv 0909.5623 v1 (September 2009). Journal: Journal of the Institute of Mathematics of Jussieu 10(2) (2011), 349-358 (search snippet of the journal record).
events.delivers: Restricted to fields whose generic type has weight 1: every such infinite stable field is separably closed. For finite weight, only the partial structural statement in Corollary 2.2, not separable closure.
events.remains: Infinite stable fields whose generic type has weight other than 1 (weight 2 or more, or infinite weight), beyond the partial statement for finite weight. The introduction describes the general statement as a longstanding conjecture.

checked_by.who: Journal of the Institute of Mathematics of Jussieu (refereed journal)
checked_by.qualification: Journal of record; the authors are model theorists working in this area
checked_by.what_they_did: Accepted and published the paper, 2010-2011 (record from a search snippet, not opened).

events.direction: Confirms the statement for weight-1 generic types; partial for finite weight.

events.what_happened: Halevi and Palacin, 'The dp-rank of abelian groups' (arXiv 1712.04503, v1 posted 12 December 2017). The abstract states that an infinite stable field of finite dp-rank is algebraically closed (opened). Published in the Journal of Symbolic Logic in 2019. Yatir Halevi's seminar 'Around the stable and dependent fields conjecture' (31 October 2018, Hebrew University) announced a proof for fields of finite dp-rank; that talk is the same result, post-dating the 2017 preprint, so I do not count it as a separate event.
events.revisions: arXiv 1712.04503 v1, 12 December 2017. Journal of Symbolic Logic, 2019 (journal record found via search snippet; not opened).
events.delivers: Restricted to stable fields of finite dp-rank: every infinite one is algebraically closed, which is stronger than separably closed, so the statement holds for that class. The Halevi-Hasson-Jahnke survey (2018) describes this case as having a surprisingly short proof.
events.remains: Infinite stable fields of infinite dp-rank.

checked_by.what_they_did: Published the paper in 2019 (not opened; record from search snippet).

events.direction: Confirms the statement for finite dp-rank (with the stronger conclusion of algebraic closure).

events.what_happened: Johnson, Tran, Walsberg and Ye, 'The etale-open topology and the stable fields conjecture' (arXiv 2009.02319, v1 posted 4 September 2020). They introduce the etale-open topology on the K-points of a K-variety and show that the topology on A^1(K) is non-discrete exactly when K is large (every smooth K-curve with a K-point has infinitely many K-points). The main application is Theorem D: if K is large and stable then K is separably closed. Theorem 3.1 extends this to virtually large fields in which every existential formula is stable. The authors call this a partial result towards the conjecture that an infinite stable field is separably closed and say that the largeness assumption 'might be necessary'. They note that Scanlon has raised whether the non-large field C(t) is stable. Published in the Journal of the European Mathematical Society, volume 26 issue 10 (2024), pp. 4033-4070, DOI 10.4171/JEMS/1345.
events.revisions: arXiv v2 30 January 2021; v3 4 August 2021; v4 7 October 2021. JEMS record: submitted 25 February 2021; published online 15 June 2023 (per the EMS page); issue 26(10), 2024.
events.delivers: Every infinite stable field that is large is separably closed (Theorem D), and every virtually large stable field in which every existential formula is stable is separably closed (Theorem 3.1). Largeness is the restriction: it excludes the non-large fields, which include finite, number and function fields.
events.remains: Every infinite stable field that is not large (or not virtually large). This includes C(t), which the authors single out as the open test case, and every non-large stable field in general.

checked_by.who: Journal of the European Mathematical Society (refereed journal)
checked_by.qualification: Journal of record; peer review by the journal
checked_by.what_they_did: Accepted and published the paper (EMS record: published 15 June 2023; volume 26 issue 10, 2024).

checked_by.who: Elliot Kaplan, Angus Matthews and Erik Walsberg
checked_by.qualification: Model theorists; Walsberg is a co-author of the original paper, so this is not an independent check
checked_by.what_they_did: Gave a substantially simplified proof of the large-stable-fields theorem in a general topological setting, stating that the proof of the first result is simplified (arXiv 2607.16942, July 2026).

events.direction: Confirms the statement for large fields, and for virtually large fields under the existential-stability hypothesis.

events.what_happened: Charlotte Bartnick, 'Embedding stable groups into algebraic groups' (arXiv 2510.24504, posted 28 October 2025). Adapts a Bouscaren-Delon argument to show that type-definable connected groups in a given stable theory of fields embed into an algebraic group, under a condition on definable closure. Covers separably closed fields of arbitrary imperfection degree and differentially closed fields. The abstract does not mention the stable fields conjecture (opened).
events.delivers: Results about definable groups inside stable theories of fields that are already known to be separably closed or differentially closed. Makes no claim about which infinite fields are stable.
events.direction: Does not bear on the statement. It assumes stability and does not decide which fields are stable.

events.what_happened: Will Johnson (Fudan University), 'Large fields, Galois groups, and NIP fields', seminar at Oxford on Thursday 30 April 2026. The listed abstract says 'Stable large fields are separably closed.' and 'Conjecturally, any stable or NIP infinite field should be large.' It is a talk restating the 2020 large-field theorem and stating a conjecture; I found no written argument for the conjecture.
events.delivers: Nothing new: restates the large-field theorem of Johnson, Tran, Walsberg and Ye. Conjectures that every infinite stable field is large, which together with that theorem would imply the statement. Not proved in the listing.
events.doubts: The stronger claim is conjectural and the listing gives no argument for it.
events.direction: Conjectural strengthening: every infinite stable field should be large, which would imply the statement. Does not prove anything.

events.what_happened: Elliot Kaplan, Angus Matthews and Erik Walsberg, 'Building trees in large fields' (arXiv 2607.16942, math.LO, submitted 18 July 2026). Main result: large rosy fields are bounded. Also simplifies the proofs of two earlier results, that large stable fields are separably closed (Johnson, Tran, Walsberg, Ye) and that large simple fields are bounded, in a general topological setting. The introduction cites Johnson, Tran, Walsberg and Ye and says 'virtually large stable fields are separably closed'.
events.delivers: (a) New, but about rosy fields: large rosy fields are bounded. (b) A simpler proof, not a new class, that large stable fields are separably closed. Only the large class is covered by (b).
events.remains: The whole statement, and in particular every non-large infinite stable field.
events.direction: Re-proves the known large-field case. Does not move the non-large case.

events.what_happened: James Freitag and Scott Mutchnik, 'A counterexample to the stable forking conjecture' (arXiv 2609.00436, 31 August 2026). The authors state that they use ChatGPT to find a counterexample to the stable forking conjecture of Hart, Kim and Pillay (1996). This concerns a different conjecture. It is not about fields. Per secondary summaries (not verified in the text I read), the counterexample is a theory of an infinite-dimensional vector space over a noncommutative division ring. The preprint is unrefereed.
events.delivers: A counterexample to the stable forking conjecture, as the authors state it. Says nothing about whether infinite stable fields are separably closed; the object is a division-ring theory, and this statement concerns commutative fields.
events.doubts: Not peer reviewed (21 pages). The AI attribution is inconsistent inside the paper (see ai and disputes). Secondary sources say independent verification had not been reported as of 7 September 2026; one tracker calls the result provisional (search snippets, not opened). No formal certificate found.
events.direction: Counterexample to a different conjecture (stable forking), if correct. No direction on the stable fields statement.
events.object: Per secondary summaries (not verified in the text I read): the theory of an infinite-dimensional vector space over the division ring of fractions of the quantum graph algebra of the random graph, a supersimple theory whose forking is not witnessed by stable formulas. Explicit construction, not a field.

Section 1.1 says they prompted ChatGPT with a detailed series of prompts that encoded the restrictions on a counterexample. A footnote says the arguments 'were based on proofs generated using JF's ChatGPT account'. This is for the stable forking conjecture, not the stable fields statement.

The same section says the proofs of the relevant facts 'have been written entirely by the authors' and that AI was used for proofreading. The paper does not reconcile these. This is for the stable forking conjecture, not the stable fields statement.

disputes.summary: The AI role in the Freitag-Mutchnik preprint (arXiv 2609.00436) is stated inconsistently. The abstract says 'Using ChatGPT 5.6'. Section 1.1 says 'AI-generated result proven with the help of GPT-5.6 Sol' and that the proofs were 'written entirely by the authors'. A footnote says the arguments 'were based on proofs generated using JF's ChatGPT account'. The model is named differently in different places. This concerns the stable forking conjecture, not this statement, and I did not pick a reading.

Date of the JEMS publication of Johnson, Tran, Walsberg and Ye. The EMS page gives 'Published 15 June 2023' and the volume is 2024 (26 issue 10). Per section 5.1 the event is dated to the first public written argument, the 2020 arXiv v1, so the journal date does not move it into the window. Recorded so that a reader counting by journal date sees the discrepancy.

summary: The statement is one universal claim: every infinite field with a stable first-order theory is separably closed. The Wikipedia entry I checked (the live page, not the January 2024 revision) matches the statement given. I found no proof and no counterexample of this claim, before or after 26 January 2024, in any source I could reach. The sources that treat it as current all describe it as open: the Johnson, Tran, Walsberg and Ye introduction (2020), Will Johnson's Oxford talk of 30 April 2026, and the Kaplan-Matthews-Walsberg paper of July 2026. The record contains a chain of partial results, each restricted to a class: omega-stable (Macintyre 1971), superstable (Cherlin and Shelah 1980), bounded (Poizat, year unverified), a characteristic-p Artin-Schreier property (Scanlon, 1999 note), weight-1 generic types and finite weight (Krupinski and Pillay, September 2009; journal 2011), finite dp-rank (Halevi and Palacin, December 2017; journal 2019), and large fields (Johnson, Tran, Walsberg and Ye, September 2020; JEMS 2024). The only event dated inside the window on this statement is Kaplan-Matthews-Walsberg (18 July 2026), which simplifies the large-field proof and proves a separate result about large rosy fields; it adds no new class. The JEMS publication in 2024 is not dated into the window, since the first public written argument is the 2020 preprint (section 5.1). The only AI-credited result in the period, Freitag and Mutchnik (arXiv 2609.00436, 31 August 2026), is a counterexample to the stable forking conjecture. Its object is a theory over a noncommutative division ring, per secondary summaries I did not verify, and I found nothing in its text I read that touches commutative fields. Its AI attribution is internally inconsistent (see disputes). On AI for this statement, I searched across the mathematics, AI-tracker, OpenAI, formalisation, and model-theory channels and found no AI involvement in any event on it. For the human-authored events the sources I read name no system, so none_found is true, with the caveat that for JTWY I read the introduction and body but not the final part of the text (acknowledgements not confirmed). The OpenAI roundup of August 2026 (Astra, ten advances) was not reachable directly (403) and press coverage lists no model-theory item. Close calls: (i) whether a partial result counts toward the problem is for the judging pass; I record only the class each one covers. (ii) The April 2026 talk's conjectural claim that every infinite stable field should be large would imply the statement if proved. It is not proved. (iii) Duret's conditional, that the simple fields conjecture implies this statement, has no date I could establish.
competing_reading: One could read the large-field theorem (Johnson, Tran, Walsberg, Ye), its 2026 simplification, and Poizat's bounded case as together covering the classes in which stable fields are known to occur, and so count the problem as largely settled. Against that: the statement quantifies over every infinite stable field, and the non-large, unbounded case, including C(t) as Scanlon asked, is untouched; the authors and the 2026 talk both describe the general case as open. On the AI side, one could count the Freitag-Mutchnik preprint as an AI result on 'stable' theory because the word matches. It concerns stable forking, not stable fields, so I do not count it here.
what_would_settle_it: Decision on whether C(t) is stable (Scanlon's question, which the JTWY introduction records and I found no resolution of). A proof that every infinite stable field is large, which is the conjectural strengthening in the April 2026 talk. A proof for the remaining non-large fields, or a verified counterexample: an infinite stable field that is not separably closed. For the AI side, independent verification of arXiv 2609.00436 and the authors' full account of who wrote which proof; neither changes this statement.
